claims.text: Rapid heating and cooling of fixed, greater-than-five-element noble-metal precursor mixtures typically yields mixed-phase or elementally segregated nanoparticles.
The controlled intervention is to slow the thermal ramp slightly by adding a short, moderate-temperature dwell before final nucleation.
A short pre-nucleation dwell or gentle thermal gradient enhances atomic interdiffusion relative to rapid nucleation.
Enhancing interdiffusion through ramp-rate modulation promotes formation and retention of a single-phase solid solution instead of phase separation or segregation.
High temperature can produce uniform mixtures of multiple elements, while rapid cooling can retain a nonequilibrium single solid solution by suppressing secondary phases.
Relevant rapid-synthesis conditions span heating pulses from tens of milliseconds to seconds, peak temperatures around 1100–2000 K, and cooling rates around 10^4–10^5 K/s.
Carbon substrates can support rapid synthesis of multielement HEA nanoparticles.
The intervention will improve the homogeneity of elemental distributions in the nanoparticles.
Elemental homogeneity and crystallographic uniformity can be evaluated by EDS mapping, XRD, and TEM.
A brief dwell temporally balances an initial rapid nucleation burst with additional time for atomic diffusion.
Greater atomic mobility permits rearrangement that mitigates kinetic trapping of segregated or secondary phases.
The adjusted thermal profile will reduce elemental segregation relative to the unmodified rapid-cycle baseline.
The adjusted thermal profile will improve crystal-structure uniformity relative to the baseline.
The adjusted thermal profile will produce a narrower particle-size distribution.
The intervention is applicable only in compositional regimes where elemental mobility is limited by rapid thermal cycling.
The applicable processing window must avoid high-temperature decomposition and excessive particle coalescence.
Overly slow ramps or overly long dwell times can cause particle growth, agglomeration, or decomposition.
Phase-homogeneity improvements may vary with composition because elemental interactions and mobility jointly influence HEA phase formation.
